summary:
A trans visitor to Ucayali faces the national framework of Peru, which governs the region directly and carries no local override. The April 2025 Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents bars any person from entering or using a public sanitary service that does not correspond to their 'biological sex', with narrow listed exceptions for custody, for situations requiring medical attention, and for accompanying an elderly person, a child under 12 or a person with disabilities. The same package prohibits inclusive signage such as 'women in their diversity'.

The measure passed the national Congress in stages. In February 2025 the Women and Family Commission unanimously approved a draft opinion merging bills 6506 and 8457, introduced by congressmen Jorge Montoya and Alejandro Muñante. The Plenary approved the fused law on 2 April 2025 and exempted it from a second vote. The stated trigger was a July 2023 social-media complaint about gendered restroom labels at Jorge Chávez airport in Lima.

LGTTBIQ activist Gianna Camacho, cited in national reporting on the February 2025 vote, called the measure discriminatory and warned that restroom access would come to depend on security staff's personal judgement, including identity-document checks. She noted that there is no record of sexual assault by trans women in women's restrooms.

The human-rights institute IDEHPUCP of the Pontifical Catholic University of Peru, in a legal analysis by Miriam Tovar and Gonzalo Ugarte dated 15 April 2025, holds that article 5 violates the equal-treatment and non-discrimination principle of article 2(2) of the Peruvian Constitution and article 1.1 of the American Convention on Human Rights. The authors state that the law's stated aim of preventing child sexual abuse rests on a stigmatising stereotype that implicitly presents trans people as likely restroom harassers, and that United Nations reporting shows trans people are more often victims than aggressors.

Enforcement of the restriction reaches private as well as public life. Peru's consumer-protection body dismissed a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced the policy. On television, presenter Ana María Salcedo of Willax TV publicly harassed Susel Paredes, the first openly lesbian member of Congress, telling her to 'go use the men's room'.

Violence against trans people is documented and under-recorded. A 2024 report found hate crimes rising in Peru with trans women most affected; its co-author Gianna Camacho stressed that the recorded figures are only a sub-registry. Between 2020 and 2023, 54 transgender and gender-diverse people were killed, trans women most affected.

In December 2025 three police officers, Dino Ponce, Luis Quispe and Juan León, were sentenced to 17 years' imprisonment for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín, a trans woman and LGBTI activist. The attack took place nearly 20 years earlier, and the case followed years of litigation. It was Peru's first conviction in a case motivated by sexual discrimination, and, per BBC News Mundo, the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region's history. The case reached the Court through the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights.

The Inter-American Court of Human Rights held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity falls under protected personal autonomy and that states must guarantee trans people's full rights. Peru's Congress voted in 2017 to strip LGBT protections from the new Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, with Popular Force and Alliance for Progress members carrying the repeal after an April Constitutional Committee vote and amid a petition claiming one million signatures. The outcome left Peru one of only three South American countries, with Paraguay and Guyana, lacking LGBT anti-discrimination coverage in hate-crime law.

Two protective developments sit on the record. In June 2024 Peru's health authorities removed outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, a change described as a step toward dignity for trans patients in healthcare settings. In July 2025 a Lima constitutional court, after an activist legal challenge, ruled an anti-equality decree unconstitutional.

Speech and association are constrained. Vague child-protection articles in the April 2025 law, including an article 4 ban on media and advertising content, enable censorship of identity, artistic and educational material, and the minimum sentence for obscenity was raised from three years to four years. Human Rights Watch states that child protection is a pretext for repression and the scapegoating of trans people.

Ucayali itself has no recorded local ordinance, incident series or enforcement pattern. The national bathroom restriction, the Penal Code gap and the national violence figures are the operative risk factors for a trans visitor in the region; local application of the 2 April 2025 rule is not documented in the sources available here.
tangentialFactors:
The bathroom restriction is part of a national pattern rather than an isolated measure, and its reach beyond state facilities is demonstrated by the dismissal of a trans woman's discrimination complaint against a gym that enforced it. A visitor should expect the rule to be applied by private security staff, not only by government personnel, with the practical consequence that access decisions may rest on personal judgement rather than a fixed procedure.

The 2017 repeal of LGBT coverage from the Penal Code's hate-crime provisions leaves trans people without that specific protection, while a 2024 report records rising hate crimes with trans women most affected and its author Gianna Camacho describing the official figures as a sub-registry. Recorded killings of 54 transgender and gender-diverse people between 2020 and 2023 indicate that official statistics understate the violence actually experienced.

The December 2025 sentence of three police officers for the rape and torture of Azul Rojas Marín shows both that accountability is possible and that it has historically been slow: the attack was nearly two decades old, the case took years of litigation, and it became the Inter-American Court of Human Rights' first torture-by-discrimination case in the region. Police involvement in the underlying offence is therefore a relevant factor for a trans visitor in any interaction with law enforcement.

Hostility is present in public institutional settings as well as in private commerce. The national institute IDEHPUCP recorded dehumanising comparisons made on the floor of Congress by congressman Lizarzaburu, and presenter Ana María Salcedo used national television to instruct Susel Paredes to 'go use the men's room'. Such statements indicate the level of public acceptance that a trans visitor may encounter when challenging a facility refusal.

Peru's alignment with regional human-rights standards is contested rather than absent. The Inter-American Court of Human Rights has held in Advisory Opinion OC-24/17 that gender identity is protected personal autonomy, and a Lima constitutional court struck down an anti-equality decree in July 2025, yet the April 2025 statutory restriction coexists with those protections and the 2024 removal of pathologising terminology from health guidance.

Censorship risk extends beyond facilities. The April 2025 child-protection articles, including the article 4 media and advertising ban and the raised obscenity minimum sentence, enable suppression of identity-related artistic, educational and media material, and Human Rights Watch identifies child protection as a pretext for the scapegoating of trans people.
localsOnly:
Ucayali has no recorded local ordinance, incident series or enforcement pattern specific to trans people. Residents of the region live under the national framework: the 2 April 2025 bathroom provision of the Law that Strengthens the Right to Sexual Integrity of Children and Adolescents, the 2017 removal of LGBT coverage from the Penal Code's hate-crime provisions, and the national violence and health-guidance record.

Local healthcare settings were affected by the June 2024 decision of Peru's health authorities to remove outdated pathologising terminology for gender diversity from official health guidance, a change described as a step toward dignity for trans patients. Whether that guidance has been implemented in Ucayali's health services is not established in the sources available here.

The gym dispute and the airport restroom complaint show that enforcement of the bathroom rule is driven by private security and institutional staff decisions, including identity-document checks, as Gianna Camacho warned in February 2025. Residents in Ucayali who challenge a refusal face the same evidentiary problem, and the region's trans population has no documented local complaint series against institutional enforcement.

Local legal protection is limited. Article 5 of the April 2025 law binds Ucayali as part of national territory, and there is no evidence in the sources reviewed of a regional or provincial authority declining to apply it, nor of a local court ruling on its constitutionality. The July 2025 constitutional ruling against an anti-equality decree was delivered in Lima, not in Ucayali.
outOfScopeNotes:
No source in the available inventory reports an incident, complaint, enforcement action or local ordinance in Ucayali specifically. The regional risk assessment therefore rests on the national framework of Peru and on enforcement patterns documented in the capital and in national media; direct evidence of how article 5 is applied in Ucayali is unresolved and not sourced here.

Unresolved in the sources reviewed: whether identity-document checks are required in practice when a facility refuses a trans person, and whether any Ucayali institution has published a restroom or facility policy under the 2 April 2025 law. Gianna Camacho's February 2025 warning that access would depend on security staff's personal judgement describes a foreseeable risk, not a documented local procedure.

Unresolved: whether the June 2024 health-guidance revision has been incorporated into the clinical practice of health services in Ucayali, and whether trans residents in the region have filed complaints over the 2017 repeal of hate-crime protections. The sources reviewed give national figures only, including 54 transgender and gender-diverse people killed between 2020 and 2023, with no regional breakdown for Ucayali.

Unresolved: the status of any legal challenge to the bathroom provision after the July 2025 Lima constitutional ruling against an anti-equality decree, and whether that ruling has any bearing on article 5. The inventory does not source a Peruvian court decision directly reviewing article 5, and the constitutional position of the provision therefore remains open on this record.
